near_miss.why_not: Norse sitting places allocated at a feast and Russian widow inheritance have different actions and legal contexts; the cognate woman/man/sit vocabulary does not establish a phrase.

near_miss.why_not: Norse bjúgra rifja concerns a projectile penetrating a man; Russian крутым ребрам concerns whipping a horse. Ribs is cognate, but curvature is anatomically ordinary and the modifiers are not demonstrated cognates; insufficient evidence for inheritance.

near_miss.why_not: Close reading of bitu ... vápn and searches for Greek δάκνω yield a comparable biting-weapon image at Aeschylus Septem 399, but the biting verbs are not cognate and a second shared lexical component is absent. Slab partners instead refer to splitting, fortifications, or chains; no inherited equation justified.

Norse nóttina ... myrkt and Serbian ноћи ... мрака have cognate night and darkness vocabulary, but the Norse temporal predication and Serbian lyric possessive image/polyptoton differ. Search results show routine Norse narrative nightfall; darkness is an inherent attribute of night, insufficiently distinctive for inheritance.

The repeated Norse myrkt af nótt construction is ordinary narrative circumstance; Serbian мрклој ноћи мрака elaborates lyric darkness. Additional Norse attestations confirm usage but do not establish a shared poetic formula across branches. See also BS-5c85e.

near_miss.lead: Poetry as mead; request for hearing
near_miss.why_not: The slab partners contain a Christian scriptural eye/ear formula or a comic reflection on fortune, not poetic mead. Wider Vedic evidence is recorded separately as a search lead; asking for attention alone is generic.

Cognate vefr / ὑφαίνω carries a textile metaphor, but Norse vefr darraðar describes battle whereas Greek μῆτιν ὕφαινον describes planning; other Greek anchors concern actual weaving. Homeric searches confirm weaving plans and speeches, not the same battle collocation. A shared productive metaphor is insufficient to reconstruct this phrase.

near_miss.why_not: Norse infant sprinkling and naming and Armenian baptism superficially align; Armenian explicitly names Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Christian transmission and different syntax prevent an inherited Indo-European phrase claim.

Norse dag ok nótt promises continuing oversight; Herodotus describes converting nights into days to evade an oracle. Only night is an assured lexical match and the temporal contrast is universal; contexts do not support a distinctive inherited merism.
Norse verse complains of a defective axe; Homer describes fighting with sharp axes. Shared weapon vocabulary does not preserve a corresponding epithet or verbal construction, and the contexts differ.

Norse waters teem with fish; Irish threat says waters will not give their fish. Irish usce is water, iasc fish, and tibridis a conditional/plural form of do-beir, not a cognate of Norse uddi. The ecological association and different verbal relations do not establish inherited phrasing.

search_lead.cognate: The second member of Óðin-mjǫð (accusative singular mjǫðr) and Vedic mádhvā (instrumental singular mádhu-) continue *médʰu, honey/mead.
search_lead.argument: The Norse poet bears Óðinn’s mead, an explicit designation of his praise poetry; Vedic asks that these utterances be filled with honey. Both apply cognate honey/mead material to poetic utterance. Worth reviewing as a shared poetic figure, though there is no exact shared two-word collocation: Norse identifies song with mead, Vedic fills words with honey. The mythological Norse compound and the Vedic ritual setting must not be collapsed into an identical formula.
